title: Choose the visual world for the Apex Cybersecurity redesign
question: The roll assigned the NIST Framework Profile. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: The Framework Profile
options.lineage: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: the six-function wheel, outcome IDs like DE.CM-01, profile tables
options.thesis: Apex is the one certified Chicago vendor that covers all six NIST functions, so the site is laid out as a framework profile.
materials: profile tables on a strict baseline
options.viewport: A large interactive six-segment CSF wheel beside the headline 'Govern to Recover. One certified partner.' Pick a function and Apex's services for it come up. MBE badge and the incident line stay in the top bar.
options.risk: If the wheel looks like decoration rather than a working index, it reads as a compliance brochure.

raised.raise: Function colors fill whole page bands at full saturation, not small chips on white.
A live 24-hour watch line shows Chicago time and 'Security Conservators on watch', so 'now' is always visible.
No cards or boxes: hierarchy comes from the baseline grid, weight and color only.
Every diagram and table is numbered and captioned like a published figure (Fig. 1, Table 2).

options.label: The Capability Statement
options.lineage: Public-sector vendor capability statements and Statements of Qualifications
options.thesis: The website as the capability statement buyers already file: core competencies, differentiators, certifications and contacts, laid out as a bid-ready document.
options.viewport: A one-page capability statement fills the screen: name, MBE certification, the core-competency list, and a 'Download capability statement' button.
options.risk: This is the most familiar choice and where most government-vendor sites end up. It's safe, but it won't stand out.

options.label: Metro Typographic Tiles
options.lineage: Metro design language: flat color tiles and very large lowercase type
options.thesis: Services become flat color tiles with oversized lowercase headlines that run off the edge of the screen.
options.viewport: A side-scrolling row of service tiles, with 'protect' cropped off the right edge.
options.case: Clear to read, but procurement buyers have no particular connection to it. Loses to the NIST profile on both counts.
options.kept: Commit fully to color: function colors fill whole regions.
options.risk: Can look like a 2012 Windows tribute.

options.label: Rhythm Machine Step Row
options.lineage: Early-80s drum machine with a sixteen-step row and a moving chase light
options.thesis: 24/7 monitoring shown as a chase light running across a row of step keys.
options.viewport: A row of 24 hour-keys with a light moving across it.
options.case: Shows 'always on' well, but it's a musical instrument. Buyers won't recognize it, and it says nothing about scope.
options.kept: Always show where 'now' is: the live watch line.

options.label: Cracktro Scroller
options.lineage: Demoscene title screens: bitmap type over a drifting black starfield
options.thesis: Services as layered lines of bitmap text, with depth showing priority.
options.viewport: One ivory line of text, still, over drifting grey dots.
options.case: Leans straight into the hacker look this audience distrusts.
options.kept: Never box content in; let the type create the hierarchy.

options.label: Curved-Crease Shell
options.lineage: Folded-paper geometry: one curved crease that makes a rigid shell
options.thesis: One line that creates structure: a single crease standing in for a single partner.
options.viewport: A cream disc folding into a saddle shape under the headline.
options.case: Elegant, but abstract. A procurement officer can't see services in it.
options.kept: Number every figure like a published plate.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A typical security-company site, done to a high standard.
canonCard.viewport: A data-center photo with a headline over it, a 'Get a consultation' button, and service cards below.
canonCard.risk: Looks like every competitor on purpose.
